p.src: Master and disciples traveled on, enjoying the sights of the Dragon Boat season and idly passing the festival of the Fifth Day, when suddenly another lofty mountain appeared to bar their way. The elder reined in his horse, turned, and called, “Wukong, there is a mountain ahead. I fear monsters may appear again, so you must be on your guard.” Pilgrim and the others said, “Rest easy, Master. We have devoted our lives and pledged our loyalty; what monsters need we fear?” The elder was delighted to hear this. He cracked his whip to urge on the fine steed, loosening the reins to hasten the dragon-horse. In a short while they had climbed the mountain ridge. Raising their heads to look, they beheld indeed:

p.src: The four travelers entered the mountain and proceeded slowly for a long while until they had crossed its summit. Descending the western slope, they came to a stretch of level country. Zhu Bajie, eager to show his vigor, made Friar Sand carry the baggage while he raised his rake in both hands and went ahead to drive the horse onward. But the horse was not at all afraid of him. No matter how the fool clucked and smacked at it, it continued at an unhurried pace. Pilgrim said, “Brother, why are you driving it so? Just let it walk at its leisure.” Bajie said, “It is nearly dark. We have been traveling through the mountain all day and our bellies are empty. Let us all quicken our pace, find a household, and beg some vegetarian food.” Hearing this, Pilgrim said, “If that is so, let me make it go faster.” He brandished the golden-hooped staff and gave a shout. The horse bolted with the reins flying loose and sped like an arrow along the level road ahead.

p.src: Why, you may ask, was the horse unafraid of Bajie yet frightened of Pilgrim? Five hundred years earlier, Pilgrim had been appointed by the Jade Emperor to tend horses in the Imperial Stables of the Great Heaven, under the official title Protector of the Horses. Thus the tradition has endured to this day that every horse fears a monkey.

p.src: Seeing how savage they were, Sanzang had no choice but to rise. Pressing his palms together before his chest, he said, “Great kings, this poor monk was sent by the Tang emperor of the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Many years and days have passed since I left Chang’an, and even if I once had a little traveling money, it has long since been spent. A monk lives solely by begging alms; how could I possess money or valuables? I beg you, great kings, to show me mercy and let this poor monk pass.” The two bandit chiefs led their men forward and said, “We have hardened our hearts like tigers and blocked this vital road expressly to take money and valuables. What do you mean by asking for mercy? If you truly have no money, take off your clothes at once and leave the white horse; then we shall let you pass.” Sanzang said, “Amitabha! For this poor monk’s robe, I begged cloth from one household and needles from another, gathering it piece by piece through alms. If you strip it from me, will that not be the death of me? Those who play the hero in this life will be reborn as beasts in the next.” The bandit flew into a rage at these words, drew forth his great club, and rushed forward to strike him. The elder said nothing aloud, but thought to himself, “Pitiful fool! You boast only of your own club, knowing nothing yet of my disciple’s!” The bandit would hear no argument. Raising his club, he struck wildly at the elder’s head and face. The elder had never told a lie in his life, but in this desperate peril he had no choice but to utter a falsehood: “Great kings, please stay your hands for a moment. A young disciple of mine is just behind and will soon arrive. He has several taels of silver on him, which I shall give you.” The bandit said, “This monk knows how to save his own skin. Tie him up for now.” All the underlings set upon him together, bound him with a rope, and hung him high in a tree.

p.src: Meanwhile, the three troublemakers came hurrying after him. Bajie laughed aloud and said, “Master went awfully fast. I wonder where he is waiting for us.” Suddenly he saw the elder in the tree and added, “Just look at Master! It would have been enough merely to wait for us, but he has taken it into his head to climb a tree, catch hold of a vine, and amuse himself on a swing!” Pilgrim saw him and said, “You fool, stop talking nonsense. Can you not see that Master is hanging there? You two come slowly. Let me go and take a look.”

p.src: The splendid Great Sage hurried up a high slope and looked carefully. Recognizing a band of robbers, he secretly rejoiced: “What luck! What luck! Business has come knocking at my door.” He immediately turned away, shook himself, and transformed into a neat and tidy young monk of sixteen, dressed in a black robe and carrying a blue cloth bundle over his shoulder. Striding forward, he came to the scene and called, “Master, what has happened here? Who are all these villains?” Sanzang said, “Disciple, why do you still ask questions instead of rescuing me?” Pilgrim asked, “What trade are they in?” Sanzang said, “This band of highwaymen stopped me and demanded a toll for passage. Since I had nothing with me, they hung me here to await your arrival and see what could be done. If there is no other way, let us give them this horse.” Hearing this, Pilgrim laughed and said, “Master, you are hopeless! There may be monks everywhere under heaven, but few are as soft-skinned as you. Emperor Taizong of Tang sent you to the Western Heaven to see the Buddha. Who told you that you might give away this dragon-horse?” Sanzang said, “Disciple, what else can I do when they hang me up like this and beat me with their demands?” Pilgrim asked, “What did you tell them?” Sanzang said, “They beat me so fiercely that I had no choice but to give you away.” Pilgrim said, “Master, how utterly feckless you are! Why did you give me away?” Sanzang said, “I told them you had some traveling money, so that they would stop beating me. It was merely something I said in the moment to escape danger.” Pilgrim said, “Good, good, good! Thank you for thinking so highly of me. That is exactly how you should give me away. If you would give me away seventy or eighty times a month, old Monkey would have more business than ever.”

p.src: Seeing Pilgrim talking with his master, the bandits spread out and closed in around them, saying, “Young monk, your master says you have traveling money at your waist. Hand it over at once, and we will spare your lives; but utter so much as half a ‘no,’ and we will put an end to what remains of your lives.” Pilgrim set down the luggage and said, “Gentlemen, please do not shout. There is some traveling money in this bundle—not much, only twenty-odd ingots of horseshoe gold, twenty or thirty ingots of fine silver, and some loose pieces I have not counted. If you want it, take bundle and all, but please do not beat my master. An ancient book says, ‘Virtue is the root; wealth is the branch.’ This is merely a matter of the branch. We who have left the household can always beg for what we need. When we meet a benevolent patron who feeds monks, we receive both alms and clothing. How much could we possibly use? I ask only that you release my master, and I will respectfully present it all to you.” The bandits were delighted to hear this. “The old monk is miserly, but the young one is quite generous,” they said. “Let him down,” they ordered. His life spared, the elder leaped onto his horse and, with no thought for Pilgrim, laid on the whip and galloped straight back along the way they had come.

p.src: Pilgrim hurriedly called after him, “You are going the wrong way!” He picked up the bundle and was about to give chase. The bandits barred his way. “Where do you think you are going? Leave the traveling money, if you want to avoid torture.” Pilgrim laughed. “Let us be clear: the traveling money must be divided into three shares.” The bandit chief said, “This young monk is a shrewd one. He means to hide a little away from his master. Very well. Take it out and let us see. If there is plenty, we will give you a little to buy fruit in secret.” Pilgrim said, “Brother, that is not what I mean. What traveling money would I have? I mean that the gold and silver you two robbed from others must be shared with me.” The bandit flew into a rage. “You reckless monk! Not only do you refuse to give me anything, you turn around and demand something from me. Do not move—take this!” He swung a stout rattan cudgel and struck Pilgrim’s bare head seven or eight times. Pilgrim acted as though he had felt nothing and merely smiled ingratiatingly. “Brother, if that is how you strike, you may keep at it until next year and through the whole spring, and it still will not count as a real beating.” The bandit was astonished. “What a hard head this monk has!” Pilgrim laughed. “You flatter me. It is nothing remarkable, though it passes muster.” The bandits would hear no more; two or three of them set upon him together, raining blows. Pilgrim said, “Gentlemen, calm yourselves. Let me take it out.”

p.src: Our Great Sage reached into his ear, pulled out an embroidery needle, and said, “Gentlemen, we monks truly carry no traveling money. Let me give you this needle instead.” The bandit said, “What rotten luck! We let a rich monk go and caught this penniless bald donkey instead. Do you claim to be a tailor? What use have I for a needle?” Hearing that he did not want it, Pilgrim pinched the needle between his fingers and gave it a shake, whereupon it became a staff as thick as a bowl. The bandits were frightened. “Small as this monk is, he knows sorcery!” Pilgrim planted the staff in the ground and said, “Gentlemen, if you can lift it, I will give it to you.” Two bandits rushed forward to seize it, but, pitifully, they were like dragonflies trying to shake a stone pillar and could not move it by the slightest fraction. This staff was none other than the As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel, weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties on the scales. How could the bandits know that? The Great Sage stepped forward, picked it up with ease, twisted into a coiling-python stance, and pointed it at the robbers. “Your luck has run low, for you have met old Sun.” The bandits advanced and struck him another fifty or sixty times.

p.src: Pilgrim laughed. “Your hands must be tired from beating me. Now let old Sun give you one stroke, but do not take it seriously.” Watch him extend the staff and shake it once: it grew as thick as a well curb and seven or eight fathoms long. With one sweeping blow he knocked a man to the ground, his lips plowing into the earth, never to make another sound. The other cursed him. “You impudent bald wretch! You have no traveling money, yet you have injured one of our men.” Pilgrim laughed. “Patience, patience. Let me strike you one by one and root the lot of you out once and for all.” With another sweeping blow, he killed the second man as well. Terrified, the remaining minions threw down spears and cudgels and fled for their lives in every direction.

p.src: Now Tang Monk was galloping eastward when Eight Rules and Friar Sand stopped him. “Master, where are you going? You have taken the wrong road.” The elder reined his horse around and said, “Disciples, hurry and tell your elder brother to show mercy with his cudgel and not kill those bandits.” Eight Rules said, “Stay here, Master, and wait for me.” The idiot ran all the way to the place ahead and shouted sternly, “Elder Brother, Master says you must not beat anyone!” Pilgrim said, “Brother, when did I ever beat anyone?” Eight Rules asked, “Then where have those bandits gone?” Pilgrim said, “The others have all dispersed. Only their two leaders are sleeping here.” Eight Rules laughed. “You two plague-stricken fellows! You must have stayed up all night and exhausted yourselves. Of all the places to sleep, why choose this one?” The idiot went up beside them, looked them over, and said, “They are just like me—sleeping with their mouths wide open, so deeply that sticky drool is running out.” Pilgrim said, “Old Sun knocked the bean curd out of them with one stroke.” Eight Rules said, “Is there bean curd inside a man’s head?” Pilgrim replied, “I knocked their brains out.”

p.src: When Eight Rules heard that their brains had been knocked out, he hurried back and told Tang Monk, “The band has broken up.” Tripitaka said, “Mercy! Mercy! Which road did they take?” Eight Rules said, “They were beaten until their legs went stiff. Where could they possibly go?” Tripitaka said, “Then why did you say the band had broken up?” Eight Rules replied, “They have been beaten to death. If that is not breaking up, what is?” Tripitaka asked, “What do they look like after the beating?” Eight Rules said, “They each have a great hole in the head.” Tripitaka ordered, “Open the bundle, take a few coins of alms, and hurry over there to buy two plasters to put on them.” Eight Rules laughed. “Master, you are being absurd. A plaster may treat the sores and swellings of the living, but how could it patch the holes of the dead?” Tripitaka asked, “Were they truly beaten to death?” He flew into a rage and muttered without cease, railing now at “that macaque,” now at “that monkey.” Turning his horse around, he went with Friar Sand and Eight Rules to the dead men and saw them lying below the hillside, drenched in blood.

p.src: The elder could not bear the sight, so he ordered Bajie, “Quickly use your rake to dig a pit and bury them. I shall recite the Sutra for the Departed over them.” Bajie said, “Master, you have ordered the wrong man. It was Brother Monkey who killed them, so he ought to be made to see to their burial. Why make old Pig do the digging?” The Pilgrim, already angered by his master’s scolding, shouted at Bajie, “You wretched, lazy oaf! Go and bury them at once. Delay a moment and you shall have a taste of my staff!” The fool panicked and dug some three feet into the hillside, but below lay nothing but rock beds and roots that caught the teeth of his rake. He threw down the rake and began rooting with his snout. When he found soft ground, one thrust of his snout went two and a half feet deep. Two thrusts made a pit five feet deep. He buried the two bandits’ corpses and heaped the earth into a grave mound. Sanzang called, “Wukong, bring incense and candles so that I may offer a prayer and recite the sutra.” The Pilgrim pouted. “What nonsense! Here halfway up a mountain, with no village ahead and no inn behind, where am I to find incense and candles? Even if we had money, there is nowhere to buy them.” Sanzang said resentfully, “Away with you, monkey! I shall take a handful of earth for incense and offer my prayer.” Thus Sanzang dismounted to mourn beside a lonely grave, and the holy monk, full of benevolence, prayed over the wilderness tomb. He prayed:

Go and bury them at once. Delay a moment and you shall have a taste of my staff!”
The fool panicked and dug some three feet into the hillside, but below lay nothing but rock beds and roots that caught the teeth of his rake.
He threw down the rake and began rooting with his snout.
When he found soft ground, one thrust of his snout went two and a half feet deep.
Two thrusts made a pit five feet deep. He buried the two bandits’ corpses and heaped the earth into a grave mound.
Sanzang called, “Wukong, bring incense and candles so that I may offer a prayer and recite the sutra.”
The Pilgrim pouted. “What nonsense! Here halfway up a mountain, with no village ahead and no inn behind, where am I to find incense and candles?
Even if we had money, there is nowhere to buy them.”
Sanzang said resentfully, “Away with you, monkey! I shall take a handful of earth for incense and offer my prayer.”
Thus Sanzang dismounted to mourn beside a lonely grave, and the holy monk, full of benevolence, prayed over the wilderness tomb.
He prayed:

p.src: Hearing this, the Great Sage could not help laughing. “Master, you are altogether too heartless. For the sake of fetching your scriptures, I have spared no effort and endured untold hardships. Now that I have killed these two petty thieves, you tell them to lodge a complaint against old Monkey! Though it was my hand that struck them, I did it only for your sake. Had you not been journeying west for the scriptures, and had I not become your disciple, how would I ever have come here and killed anyone? I may as well offer them a prayer myself.” Gripping his iron staff, he thrust it three times at the grave and said, “You plague-stricken bandits, listen well! First you struck me seven or eight blows, then another seven or eight, yet they neither hurt nor itched. You roused my temper, and through an unlucky mishap I killed you. Go wherever you please to make your complaint; old Monkey truly has no fear. The Jade Emperor knows me, and the Heavenly Kings accommodate me; the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions dread me, and the Nine Luminary Star Lords fear me; the city gods of prefectures and counties kneel before me, and the Heavenly Equal of the Eastern Peak quakes at me; the ten generations of Yama Kings once served as my attendants, and the ferocious gods of the five roads once acted as my juniors. Whether among the Three Realms and Five Offices or all the rulers of the ten directions, they are my intimate acquaintances. Go and complain wherever you like!” Hearing such vicious words, Sanzang grew alarmed again. “Disciple, my prayer was meant to teach you reverence for life and make you a good and benevolent man. Why have you taken it so seriously?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, this is no matter for jesting. Let us press on while it is early and find lodging.” The elder had no choice but to mount his horse, still nursing his anger.

Pointing with his whip, Sanzang said, “Let us go there and ask for lodging.” Bajie said, “Just so.” They went to the edge of the estate and dismounted. When they looked, they found it a fine dwelling indeed. They saw:

p.src: The elder stepped forward and suddenly saw an old man emerge through the cottage gate. He met him and offered a greeting. The old man asked, “Where have you monks come from?” Sanzang replied, “This poor monk is an imperial envoy from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, bound for the Western Heaven to seek the scriptures. Passing through your honored region, I found the day growing late, and so have come expressly to your charitable house to beg one night’s lodging.” The old man smiled. “The journey from your noble country to this place is exceedingly long. How did you cross rivers and climb mountains to reach here all alone?” Sanzang said, “This poor monk has also brought three disciples with him.” The old man asked, “Where are your worthy disciples?” Sanzang pointed with his hand. “Those standing beside the main road are they.” The old man abruptly raised his head, saw their hideous faces, and hurriedly turned to go back inside. Sanzang caught hold of him. “Venerable benefactor, I beg you to show mercy and lend us lodging for one night!” The old man trembled, scarcely able to speak. Shaking his head and waving his hands, he said, “No, no, no! They do not look human! They—they—they are monsters!” Sanzang smiled placatingly. “Benefactor, pray do not be afraid. My disciples were born with such appearances, but they are not monsters.” The old man said, “Merciful heavens! One is a yaksha, one a horse-faced demon, and one the Duke of Thunder!” Hearing this, the Pilgrim shouted fiercely, “The Duke of Thunder is my grandson, the yaksha my great-grandson, and Horse-Face my great-great-grandson!” At these words the old man was scared out of his wits. His face lost all color, and he wanted only to get inside. Sanzang supported him into the thatched hall and said with a soothing smile, “Venerable benefactor, do not fear him. They are all rough fellows like this and do not know how to speak properly.”

p.src: While Sanzang was trying to reassure him, an old woman came from the rear leading a child of five or six by the hand. She asked, “Old man, why are you so frightened?” Only then did the old man call, “Old woman, bring tea.” The old woman promptly let go of the child, went inside, and brought out two cups of tea. After drinking the tea, Sanzang came down from his seat and bowed to the old woman. “This poor monk has been sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. We have only just reached your honored region and came to beg lodging at your noble house. But because my three disciples are ugly, the venerable master of the house took needless fright when he saw them.” The old woman said, “If an ugly face frightens you so badly, what would you do if you saw a tiger, jackal, or wolf?” The old man said, “Old woman, ugly human faces would be tolerable; it is their speech that is even more frightening. I said they looked like a yaksha, Horse-Face, and the Duke of Thunder, and he bellowed that the Duke of Thunder was his grandson, the yaksha his great-grandson, and Horse-Face his great-great-grandson. That is why his words terrified me.” The Tang Monk said, “No, no. The one who looks like the Duke of Thunder is my senior disciple, Sun Wukong; the one who looks like Horse-Face is my second disciple, Zhu Wuneng; and the one who looks like a yaksha is my third disciple, Sha Wujing. Though they are ugly, they observe the Buddhist teaching and have taken refuge in the good fruition. They are no malignant demons or venomous monsters, so why fear them?”

p.src: When the old couple heard their names and learned that they had embraced the true Buddhist path, they finally calmed their nerves and recovered from their fright. “Invite them in, invite them in,” they said. The elder went out and called them over, then instructed them, “This old gentleman took a strong dislike to you just now. When you go in to meet him, you must not behave discourteously; each of you must show proper respect.” Bajie said, “I am handsome and refined, nothing like Elder Brother and his wild behavior.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Were it not for your long snout, huge ears, and ugly face, you would indeed be a fine-looking fellow.” Sha Monk said, “Stop arguing. This is no place to show off your charms and cleverness. Let us go in, let us go in.” They brought their luggage and horse into the thatched hall, all saluted together, and took their seats. The good old woman immediately led the child away and ordered the rice to be cooked. She prepared a vegetarian meal, which master and disciples ate.

p.src: As evening gradually fell, the lamps were lit again, and they all sat chatting idly in the cottage. Only then did the elder ask, “May I ask your honored surname, benefactor?” The old man replied, “Yang.” He then asked his age. The old man said, “Seventy-four.” He asked again, “How many sons do you have?” The old man replied, “Only one. The child whom my wife was leading just now is my little grandson.” The elder asked that his son come and exchange bows with them. The old man said, “That wretch is unworthy of your courtesy. My fate is bitter: I failed to raise him properly, and now he is away from home.” Tripitaka asked, “Where does he make his living?” The old man shook his head and sighed. “Alas, alas! If only he were willing to earn an honest living anywhere, it would be a blessing to me. That wretch thinks of nothing but evil, neglects honest work, and delights solely in raiding homes and waylaying travelers, murdering people and setting fires. All his companions are a pack of scoundrels. He went out five days ago and has not returned yet.” Hearing this, Tripitaka scarcely dared breathe a word and thought to himself, “Perhaps he was one of those Wukong killed.” Uneasy in mind, the elder shifted in his seat and said, “Mercy! Mercy! How could such worthy parents have begotten so wicked and rebellious a son?”

p.src: The Pilgrim stepped forward and said, “Old sir, what use is a vicious, unfilial son like that, given to treachery, robbery, depravity, and lust, who only brings trouble upon his parents? Let me find him for you and beat him to death.” The old man replied, “I too would gladly be rid of him, but I have no younger heir. Worthless though he is, I must keep him to cast earth over my grave.” Sha Monk and Bajie laughed. “Brother, don’t meddle in other people’s affairs. We are not magistrates. If his family will not consent, what has it to do with us? Let us simply ask our host to grant us a bundle of straw, spread it over there for the night, and resume our journey at daybreak.” The old man rose at once and had Sha Monk fetch two bundles of rice straw from the rear garden, telling them to rest in the round thatched hut there. The Pilgrim led the horse, Bajie carried the luggage, and together with the elder they all went to rest in the hut. Of this no more need be said.

p.src: Now among that band of robbers there truly was a son of old Yang. After the Pilgrim had killed their two chiefs before the mountain early that morning, they had all fled for their lives in different directions. Around the fourth watch they gathered into a band once more and came pounding on the gate. Hearing the noise at the gate, the old man threw on his clothes and said, “Wife, those fellows have come.” His wife said, “Since they have come, go open the gate and let them into the house.” No sooner had the old man opened the gate than the whole band cried out, “We’re starving! We’re starving!” Old Yang’s son hurried inside, woke his wife, and told her to wash rice and cook a meal. There was no firewood in the kitchen, however, so he went to the rear garden to fetch some. Returning to the kitchen, he asked his wife, “Where did that white horse in the rear garden come from?” His wife replied, “It belongs to some monks from the Eastern Land who are going to fetch scriptures. They arrived last night seeking lodging. Father and Mother served them an evening vegetarian meal and had them sleep in the round thatched hut.”

p.src: Hearing this, the wretch ran out into the cottage, clapped his hands, and laughed. “Brothers, what luck! What luck! Our enemies are in my house!” The robbers asked, “What enemies?” The wretch replied, “They are the monks who killed our chiefs. They came to lodge at my house and are sleeping in the round thatched hut right now.” The robbers said, “Excellent! Excellent! We’ll seize those bald donkeys and chop every one of them into mincemeat. First, we shall gain their luggage and white horse, and second, avenge our chiefs.” The wretch said, “There is no hurry. Go sharpen your blades first. When the rice is cooked, we’ll all eat our fill and then strike together.” And indeed, some of the robbers sharpened their swords while others sharpened their spears.

p.src: When the old man heard this, he slipped quietly into the rear garden and woke Tang Monk and his three disciples. “That wretch has brought his band here. They know you are staying here and intend to harm you. Knowing you have come from afar, I cannot bear to let you be hurt. Quickly pack your luggage, and I will see you out through the rear gate.” When Tripitaka heard this, he tremblingly kowtowed his thanks to the old man. He then called for Bajie to lead the horse, Sha Monk to shoulder the luggage, and the Pilgrim to take up the nine-ringed priest’s staff. The old man opened the rear gate and let them out, then stole quietly back to the front and lay down as before.

p.src: Now the wretches sharpened their swords and spears and ate their fill. By then it was the fifth watch. They went together into the garden to look, only to find their prey gone. They hurriedly lit lamps and torches and searched for a long while, but found no trace in any direction; only the rear gate stood open. They all cried, “They’ve fled through the rear gate! They’ve fled!” With a great shout, they set off in pursuit. Each sped like a flying arrow, and only when the sun rose in the east did they finally catch sight of Tang Monk. The elder suddenly heard their shouts and looked back. Behind him came twenty or thirty men, bristling with spears and swords. He cried, “Disciples! The bandits have caught up with us. What are we to do?” The Pilgrim replied, “Don’t worry, don’t worry. Old Sun will deal with them.” Tripitaka reined in his horse and said, “Wukong, you must not hurt anyone. Just frighten them away.” But the Pilgrim would not listen. He swiftly drew his staff, turned to meet them, and called, “Where are you gentlemen going?” The robbers cursed him. “You insolent bald wretch! Give us back our chiefs’ lives!” The wretches formed a ring around the Pilgrim and hacked and thrust wildly at him with swords and spears. The Great Sage gave his gold-banded cudgel a shake, making it as thick as a rice bowl, and struck the bandits until they scattered like stars before the clouds: those who met it died, and those it swept away perished; those it knocked against suffered broken bones, and those it merely grazed had their skin torn; the cleverer few escaped, while all the fools went to see King Yama.

p.src: Seeing so many men struck down while he sat on his horse, Tripitaka panicked and spurred westward. Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk followed hard at his stirrups. The Pilgrim asked one of the wounded bandits who was still alive, “Which one is old Yang’s son?” Groaning, the bandit told him, “Grandfather, it’s the one in yellow.” The Pilgrim stepped forward, snatched away a sword, and cut the head from the man in yellow. Holding the dripping head in his hand, he put away his iron cudgel, bounded off on the clouds, caught up with Tang Monk’s horse, and raised the head before him. “Master, this is old Yang’s rebellious son. Old Sun has brought you his head.” At the sight, Tripitaka turned pale with terror and tumbled from his horse, crying, “You outrageous ape! You’ve frightened me to death! Take it away! Take it away!” Bajie stepped forward and kicked the head off to the roadside, then used his rake to heap earth over it.

p.src: Sha Wujing set down the luggage, helped the Tang Monk to his feet, and said, “Master, please get up.” Once the elder had collected himself on the ground, he began reciting the Tight-Fillet Spell. It squeezed Wukong until his ears burned red, his face flushed, his eyes bulged, and his head reeled. Rolling on the ground, he cried over and over, “Stop reciting! Stop!” The elder recited it more than ten times and still would not stop. Wukong somersaulted and stood on his head, unable to bear the pain, and cried, “Master, please forgive me!
